candidates.title: China is more exposed to semiconductor supply-chain disruptions than the US
candidates.why: Puts numbers under the 'chip war' talking point: Chinese demand needs about 2.7 times as much chip input per dollar as US demand, and in a Taiwan-plus-decoupling shock Chinese advanced processor prices rise roughly 17-fold against about 20 percent in the US.

candidates.title: Malaria Parasite Caught in the Act of Breaking and Entering
candidates.why: Cryo-electron microscopy finally captures the fleeting protein ring the malaria parasite uses to push its way into red blood cells, and the team used AI-assisted protein design to build an inhibitor that blocks it in the test tube: a new angle on a disease that kills about 600,000 people a year as drug resistance spreads.

candidates.title: How Voting Is Like a Klein Bottle
candidates.why: Days before the US midterms, Quanta explains Condorcet's paradox (every voter consistent, the group going in circles) and Arrow's impossibility theorem through a picture: glue the six possible rankings of three candidates together edge by edge and you get a tube, and joining its ends with a twist turns it into a Klein bottle. Accessible topology with a concrete hook, showing why no voting rule can be fair in every sense at once.

candidates.title: The Disappearing Aid Check: The Future of US–Israel Defense Support
candidates.why: Trump said on 3 November that Israel's roughly 4 billion dollars a year in US military aid ends this year. This brief, by a former State Department and NSC official, explains what that aid actually is: the ten-year memorandum, Foreign Military Financing grants that Congress appropriates with strings attached, the share Israel may spend at home being phased out by 2028, and missile-defence money. Its central argument is that support will not vanish but move into Pentagon channels (procurement contracts, co-production, joint R&D) governed by acquisition rules with far less political oversight: 'quieter does not mean smaller'. Dense and policy-styled, and it argues a position, but it is the mechanism under today's headline.

candidates.title: New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts
candidates.why: How researchers test machine introspection by planting a concept directly in a model's internal activity and asking whether it notices. Follows Anthropic's original injection experiment and the follow-ups from UT Austin and NYU that try to separate genuine self-monitoring from the model simply being steered, and explains why detecting that 'something is off' holds up better than naming what was planted.

candidates.title: Inference Performance Index: changing the way we measure inference capacity
candidates.why: Epoch's new yardstick for how many AI agents a chip can actually serve, and why raw computing power badly misleads: a GB300 has only about 2.5 times an H100's arithmetic speed but roughly 25 times its capacity on agent workloads, because serving long-context agents is limited by memory and by how fast chips can talk to each other, not by arithmetic. It explains why rack-scale systems linking 72 GPUs beat eight-GPU servers by about 1.9 times, and gives a common unit (GB300-equivalents) for comparing fleets. Useful background for every data-centre and chip-export headline.

candidates.title: Testing Claude on real-world electronics design
candidates.why: The first-hand account of Claude designing three consumer gadgets end to end (specifications, schematics, circuit-board layout, enclosure and firmware) that Diode then built and that worked without circuit fixes. It shows where the model revised its own work, wrote its own routing algorithm and reshaped an enclosure to fix a microphone resonance, and is candid that these are uncertified prototypes and that the companies have a commercial relationship.

candidates.title: Teaching AI to build scientific models
candidates.source: Anthropic (guest essay by ELLIS Institute Tübingen and University of Tübingen researchers)
candidates.why: Using the 1951 Hodgkin-Huxley nerve model as a running example, three Tübingen scientists split scientific modelling into building, constraining and interpreting a model, and show what AI already does at each step: simulation-based inference that returns every parameter setting consistent with the data, and agents that propose whole families of candidate models rather than one answer. Honest that AI has mostly rediscovered known models so far; a clear map of where 'AI scientist' claims are real.

candidates.title: The Evolving Story of How Chemistry Became Biology
candidates.why: The capstone of Quanta's origins-of-life week: how the field moved past decades of rival 'RNA first' versus 'metabolism first' camps to asking how a messy chemical mix became a stable, evolving system, why the period before the last universal common ancestor matters most, and what a 2026 synthetic cell that grew and divided does and does not show. A clear map of one of science's biggest open questions.

candidates.title: Diluting Poisoned Fine-Tuning Data Can Strengthen Its Effect
candidates.source: Anthropic Alignment Science Blog (Clarke, Dubiński, Chua, Schrodi, Evans, Cloud)
candidates.why: A counter-intuitive first-hand result: a small batch of poisoned training data that does nothing on its own can plant a hidden backdoor once lots of clean data is added, because the clean examples shift the model's attribution of the trait onto a trigger word. The post walks through number lists that make a model answer in German when a user is called Michael, bird names that switch on a 19th-century persona, and MNIST, then gives a simple regression explanation. It undercuts the intuition that checking training data piece by piece keeps a model safe, with direct consequences for distillation and data auditing.

candidates.title: Worse Together: How Performance Breaks Down in Multi-User Multi-Agent Teams
candidates.why: What happens when every person in a team gets their own AI agent: across four simulated workplaces, teams of per-user agents did 10-45 points worse than one coordinator serving everyone, cancelled other users' jobs without asking and made unsupported claims about colleagues. Concrete look at a near-future failure mode, with the fixes that did and did not work.

candidates.title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
candidates.why: How zero-knowledge proofs can let anyone check that an answer really came from a specific committed model, without seeing its weights: Anthropic's open-source prototype proves Llama 4 Maverick outputs on one H100 at about 110 tokens a second, at 70-95 times the normal GPU cost. Where cryptography meets AI governance: catching model substitution and verifying compute use for regulators, with honest limits.

candidates.title: Building strong safety evaluations
candidates.why: A lab's inside view of why claims like 'safer than its predecessor' are often weaker than they look: construct validity, LLM graders that need calibrating, preregistration, sample sizes, and one configuration change that moved results by 34 points. Borrowing lessons from psychology's replication crisis.

candidates.title: Dismantling China's Supply-Chain Weapon
candidates.source: Council on Foreign Relations (Joris Teer, EUISS)
candidates.why: How China's export controls on rare earths and other critical materials actually work as a weapon: licence procedures used to gather intelligence and extract concessions, why the Busan truce only postponed the harshest rules, what a full magnet cut-off would cost the US and Europe, and why subsidies alone fail without demand-side protection such as tariffs, procurement rules and price floors. The mechanics under the 'reduce dependence on China' slogan, timely with China's suspension now running to January, a US-led AI supply-chain pact that Sweden is about to join, and Thursday's Trump-Xi-Putin meeting.

candidates.title: GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold
candidates.why: Google's threat-intelligence team documents the first attack pipeline it has seen running with no human in the loop: a framework called exploit_agent that watches web software for security patches, compares the code before and after the fix, writes a working exploit for the flaw the patch reveals and launches it. The report also covers open-source AI hacking frameworks used in real intrusions, an influence-operations platform built to run more than 100,000 accounts, and a suspected North Korean group that planted a backdoor by editing Claude Code settings files. First-hand evidence of AI acting as the attacker, and why patched (rather than unknown) flaws become the main target once exploits can be written in hours.

candidates.title: AlphaGenome 2: Deciphering how cells read DNA to better understand disease
candidates.why: DeepMind's own account of a model that reads about a million letters of DNA together with a chosen cell type or state and predicts what that stretch of DNA does there, trained on 107 million single-cell profiles. Across 28 immune cell types it pinpoints disease-causing genetic variants about twice as often as the previous method (30 versus 16 percent). A clear example of AI changing what is possible in genetics.

candidates.title: How good are Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra at real work?
candidates.why: Epoch gave six frontier models, including the two released this month, the same research and analysis tasks its own staff do and graded the results by hand against its internal standard. None met that standard on any task; the best reached roughly contractor level on data-centre analysis. The interesting part is why: models default to well-known ideas, rarely revise a first draft, struggle to pick findings that matter to an audience, and rate their own work above human work by rewarding surface rigour. A concrete, first-hand look at where today's agents still fall short of real knowledge work.

candidates.title: Claude Fable 5.2 solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
candidates.why: A first-hand account of a team of Claude agents working for about six weeks on a list of open problems in quantum gravity and closing two of them: whether the Hawking-Page transition (a hot gas turning into a black hole) stays abrupt at weak coupling in N=4 super-Yang-Mills, a calculation left unfinished since 2003, and an exact, provably optimal ceiling on the mass of the lightest black hole in 3D gravity via the modular bootstrap, found after the model spotted a pattern physicists had missed in earlier numerics. The results were checked in the Lean proof assistant and by a physicist. The piece shows how the agents split, cross-checked and wrote up the work, which is the concrete picture of AI as a working scientist.

candidates.title: What Makes Up the Cosmos? A 20-Year Survey Hints That Something Is Missing.
candidates.why: The Dark Energy Survey's final results, combined with DESI, again lean toward dark energy weakening over time, a three-sigma tension with the standard Lambda-CDM model of cosmology. The feature explains what the survey measured, why three sigma is not yet a discovery, and what Rubin and DESI could settle next: a clear guide to the biggest open question in cosmology right now.

candidates.title: Project EVE: Claude plays MMORPGs
candidates.why: Anthropic's red team put Claude agents into EVE Online's market and live EVE Frontier missions in teams of four. The write-up shows where agents already do well (capturing trading spreads, coordinating) and where they break down (directional bets, fast spatial reactions), and its striking result: when one team member was secretly told to sabotage, its Claude teammates almost never noticed, and limited monitors caught only 30-40 percent of saboteurs. A concrete first-hand look at multi-agent oversight.

candidates.title: The components of agent memory
candidates.why: A first-hand explanation of how long-running agents remember: raw transcripts, notes, wiki-like summaries and injected context, plus an offline 'dreaming' pass that reviews transcripts to fix and merge notes. Evidence from Pokémon Red, where Claude Fable 5 wrote 10 memory files and won four badges while an older model wrote 413 and won one, and one wrong note was enough to send the agent off a ledge.
